question:
Patient note:
A 63-year-old woman is reviewed in the operating theater holding suite this morning shortly before an open sigmoid colectomy with primary anastomosis that the colorectal service scheduled as the first case of the day; the procedure is deemed extensive because it will involve a midline laparotomy, mobilization of the left colon, and vascular ligation at the inferior mesenteric pedicle, and the anesthesia team anticipates several hours under general endotracheal anesthesia with arterial monitoring. Five days earlier she was admitted from the emergency department for a second episode of complicated diverticulitis manifesting as a persistent peri-sigmoid phlegmon and a small colovesical fistulous tract seen on contrast CT; after broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics she defervesced and her leukocytosis resolved, and the surgical plan moved forward once bowel rest, nasogastric decompression, and nutritional optimization were achieved. During this brief inpatient course she has been encouraged to dangle at the bedside but, owing to colicky abdominal pain and the presence of multiple pumps, she has actually remained in bed except for bathroom transfers with assistance, logging fewer than a hundred steps a day according to nursing flow sheets. Peripheral access proved difficult at admission, so interventional radiology placed a 5 French single-lumen power-injectable peripherally inserted central catheter in the right basilic vein on hospital day two; the dressing is clean and dry, and the line is presently running maintenance crystalloid at 50 mL/h. Her past month was notable for a community-acquired right-lower-lobe pneumonia diagnosed three weeks ago by her primary physician after she developed pleuritic pain and productive cough; a seven-day course of high-dose oral amoxicillin-clavulanate led to near-complete radiographic resolution, and she has had no fevers or sputum since, though a mild exertional wheeze persists that she attributes to her underlying chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. That lung condition stems from a 35-pack-year cigarette habit discontinued twelve years ago; maintenance therapy includes twice-daily inhaled budesonide-formoterol and as-needed albuterol, and her last exacerbation requiring prednisone was nine months prior. She denies any prior episodes of venous clot, has never experienced hemoptysis or sudden dyspnea suggestive of embolus, and no first-degree relatives have suffered unexplained thrombosis or stroke at an early age. Cardiac review is negative for orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, or recent decompensation, and she has not been hospitalized for heart failure or myocardial ischemia in the past year. Beyond an uncomplicated laparoscopic cholecystectomy more than a decade ago, she has undergone no operations in recent months, and her only other chronic conditions are well-controlled hypertension and diet-managed type 2 diabetes. She takes lisinopril 10 mg daily, metformin 500 mg twice daily (held since yesterday in anticipation of contrast and anesthesia), her inhalers, calcium carbonate, and a multivitamin; she is not on estrogen therapy or corticosteroids. Vital signs on arrival: temperature 36.9 °C, blood pressure 142/78 mm Hg, heart rate 82/min regular, respiratory rate 16/min, oxygen saturation 95 % on 2 L nasal cannula that she prefers for comfort. Body mass index is 29 kg/m². She is sitting propped on pillows, appears calm, speaks in full sentences, and denies pain at rest. Jugular venous pulsation is normal, heart sounds are crisp without murmurs, lungs reveal scattered end-expiratory wheezes and faint inspiratory crackles at the right base but no egophony or increased fremitus, and room-air arterial blood gas yesterday showed pH 7.40, PaCO₂ 44 mm Hg, PaO₂ 78 mm Hg. The abdomen is soft but tender over the left lower quadrant with voluntary guarding, no rebound, and hypoactive bowel sounds; a soft Foley catheter draining clear urine is in place for fistula management. Extremities are warm, capillary refill brisk, calves are supple without pitting or cords, and no superficial varices are observed. Neurologic exam is intact, and she moves all four limbs spontaneously though she declines to ambulate because “the fistula bag tugs and hurts.” Laboratory studies drawn early this morning demonstrate hemoglobin 11.8 g/dL, hematocrit 35 %, platelets 232 × 10⁹/L, white blood cells 8.1 × 10⁹/L, sodium 137 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, creatinine 0.88 mg/dL, glucose 128 mg/dL, alanine aminotransferase 24 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 22 U/L, total bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL, international normalized ratio 1.0, and activated partial thromboplastin time 29 s. A repeat chest radiograph obtained yesterday to document pneumonia clearance shows only minimal residual right basilar streaks without consolidation, and electrocardiogram reveals normal sinus rhythm with nonspecific T-wave changes unchanged from prior. She has remained nil per os since midnight except for small sips to swallow her antihypertensive tablet. Sequential compression devices were ordered but left off overnight because she complained they aggravated her hip bursitis; they will be applied once anesthesia induction is underway, and chemoprophylaxis will be initiated according to institutional protocol after surgical hemostasis is secured.

Question: What is the patient's Caprini Score for Venous Thromboembolism?
solution:
The preoperative Caprini score sums weighted VTE risk factors:
- Age 63 (61–74 years) → 2.
- Planned open colectomy lasting >45 minutes → 2.
- Confined to bed except for assisted bathroom transfers for 5 days (≥72 hours) → 2.
- PICC in place, qualifying as central venous access → 2.
- BMI 29 kg/m² (>25) → 1.
- Pneumonia 3 weeks ago, within the 1-month pulmonary risk window → 1.
Total counting pulmonary disease once: 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 1 + 1 = 10. The distinction matters: on a Caprini form that scores chronic abnormal pulmonary function (COPD) separately from recent pneumonia, her COPD adds 1 and the total is 11.
Final answer: 10
